about: Why browsers say "Your connection is not private". Factory #30, backlog row 34, slug notprivate. One hard idea: every HTTPS site shows your browser a certificate (its ID card) that is only valid between two dates; the browser checks it, and when it can't verify it, it stops before any data is sent and shows the warning. Usual causes are boring (your device's clock is wrong, a Wi-Fi sign-in page got in the way, the site's certificate expired or is misconfigured), but sometimes someone is pretending to be the site, so on a bank, shopping or login site never click through. Sources (read 2026-11-13) in BRIEF.md section 3: Chrome Help 95669 and 95617, Chromium's own warning strings, Firefox's own warning strings, Apple Safari guide, Google's 2017 CCS paper (Acer et al.), CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements 2.3.1. Planned silences: 0.5 s after the hook (frame-0 hit), 0.6 s after 'a real card fails.' (card-fail buzz), 0.6 s after 'pretending to be the site.' (door knock), 1.2 s after 'never click through.' (hero: coral door chain snaps taut, screenshot hold). Narration-led: record the voice first and key every visual beat to its word times.

lines.text: This warning doesn't mean you're hacked.
So why does it say your connection is not private?
lines.say: So, why does it say your connection is not private?

lines.text: Every secure site shows your browser a dated ID card.
lines.say: Every secure site shows your browser a dated I D card.

lines.text: Your browser checks those dates with your own clock.
If your clock is off, a real card fails.
One Google study blamed clocks for a third on Windows.
Airport Wi-Fi does it too, until you sign in.
But sometimes, someone's pretending to be the site.
So check your clock and the Wi-Fi first.
On a banking site, never click through.
Have you ever clicked through? Yes or no.
